content:
WASHINGTON ― President Donald Trump will finally get a meeting with his favorite dictators in the same room at the same time on Thursday, with a “summit” that includes China’s Xi Jinping, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, and perhaps even North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.

What might result from the get-together is unclear, although some foreign policy experts believe the three would like to create a new world order in which they are given de facto hegemony over their respective geographical areas, with China in charge in Asia, Russia in Europe, and the United States in the Western Hemisphere.

“Trump wants to carve up the world among the three of them and over the heads of and in strategic betrayal of our longtime allies,” said Robert Kagan, a top State Department official during the Reagan administration.

Jim Townsend, a former staffer at the Pentagon and NATO, and now an analyst with the Center for a New American Security, said that worries about a repeat of the post-war Yalta conference that gave the Soviet Union control over Eastern Europe for two generations may be overblown.

“The world is laughing at Trump,” he said. “They can see right through this photo op meeting that he’s being manipulated and is actually regarded with contempt by the other two.”

Russian nationalists, for their part, have been openly cheering the coming meeting as proof of their country’s renewed relevance.

“It shows who is important in the world: We are, China and the West,” Aleksandr Dugin, a Putin supporter popular on state media, said in an interview with Radio Sputnik.

Nations not at the table, though, are less enthusiastic about the meeting in Shenzhen, which this year is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said any discussion about ending Russia’s nearly five-year war against his country without the participation of Ukraine was inappropriate.

European leaders, meanwhile, wonder why Russia would be involved at all in a “great powers” discussion. “I think that’s an unnecessary elevation of Russia to position of a global superpower, which Russia hasn’t been for a long time,” Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said this week. “It should be a meeting in the triangle of China, the U.S. and the European Union.”

While Trump has always been eager for meeting with autocrats, how ― and why ― a meeting with both Xi and Putin came to pass is unclear.

In October, the White House confirmed reporting that Putin had suggested the idea during a phone call with Trump. But earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Brazil’s socialist leader, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, had told him it was he who had proposed that Trump meet with Xi and Putin to help end the war in Ukraine, which Brazilian media had reported back in August following a call between Trump and Lula.

As to the purpose of the meeting, the White House told reporters in a weekend “background briefing” ― in which officials provide information on the condition their names not be used ― that Ukraine was not an expected topic and that the meeting would focus on reducing nuclear arms.

But as he boarded Marine One at the White House Monday to start his Asia trip, Trump himself said he expected the topic of Ukraine to come up.

“We’ll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine’s losing ― Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” he told reporters.

That was also where he mentioned the possibility of Kim ― who rarely leaves North Korea ― joining the gathering: “We might have Kim Jong Un. He may come. I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”

Trump’s White House did not respond to HuffPost questions asking what the United States might get of value with a meeting of these various dictators.

Trump critics are confident the answer will be not much.

“Depends on whether anything substantive comes out of the trilateral,” said John Bolton, a Trump national security adviser during his first term who, like others who publicly criticize Trump, has been prosecuted by Trump’s Justice Department. “I doubt it. I suspect most countries will see it as a photo op for Trump, which they may not like, but they will see it as Trump being Trump. They would be mistaken if they thought most Americans wanted any part of it.”

Jan Techau, with the Center for European Policy Analysis in Berlin, said Trump’s eagerness to mingle with dictators, particularly Putin, will not set well in Europe, where countries have been helping Ukraine since Putin invaded his neighbor in January 2022.

“It still hurts U.S. reputation and standing in some parts of the world, despite the fact we are all jaded by now,” Techau said. “The midterms have made it clear that Trump is not the same thing as the U.S. And yet, a lot of geopolitical damage is still done by Trump in America’s name.”

Trump has praised all three autocrats for years. As he ran for the presidency in 2016, he said Putin was a better leader for Russia than then-President Barack Obama was for the U.S., and has since returning to office last year tilted U.S. policy toward Russia and away from Ukraine. He has frequently lauded Xi for ruling China with an “iron fist” and has expressed his admiration for Kim, even praising how he murdered his uncle with an anti-aircraft gun.

Kagan said that Trump, while perhaps weakened domestically following the midterm elections, agrees that he can continue to hurt both the United States and allies with his foreign policy.

“His ‘new security architecture’ for Europe, for instance, would give Moscow control over how Eastern European countries can and cannot defend themselves, thus depriving a country like Poland of the essence of national sovereignty,” Kagan said. “In Asia, countries like Japan, South Korea and, especially, Taiwan cannot help but worry about a similar carving up of their region. This will hasten the breakdown of peace in the world.”
